utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rabrenovic, you wish to address us?

utterances.speaker: MR. RABRENOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I use the time in between the witness coming in now - it's got nothing to do with this matter - to raise an administrative matter? And it is this: I received your decision with respect to the acceptance of exhibits along with General Stevanovic's testimony. I think that there has been an omission in that decision and ruling and it is this: Before you interrupted my re-examination, before General Stevanovic, and here on the overhead projector two documents were shown, and as I was stopped they were returned to me, but General Stevanovic, and you can see that on the transcript, he did state his opinions. And they are important and vital because they refer to those parts of the cross-examination by Mr. Nice where he did not deal with examination-in-chief but opened up the question of Srebrenica. So it was quite logical for me to ask those questions in the re-examination because the questions had nothing to do with Serbia or General Stevanovic. Now, those two exhibits which General Stevanovic read on the overhead projector and said that he was aware of them, that the facts were correct, are the following: One was the criminal report against Drazen Erdemovic, who was tried here, and it was placed on the ELMO and it was read by General Stevanovic. It's a criminal report dated the 6th of March, 1996, in which it says -- it sets out what happened there. And the second document, the second exhibit was a public document. I had a number of them but only one was placed on the ELMO just before we adjourned, and that was the press conference of the federal information minister, dated February 2000, in which the federal minister of information, in the name of the government, informs the public about the apprehension of the perpetrators of the crime in Srebrenica, the members of that infamous 10th Sabotage Detachment. Now, the fact that -- the very fact that the minister of information does this on behalf of in the name of the government at that time challenges and contests the stand of Mr. Nice as to what happened in Srebrenica to the present time. That is why I should like to have these two exhibits brought out again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are there any numbers attached?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we can look at them. We'll look into the matter, and if it requires a change in the decision, then we'll make the change.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These exhibits did not have numbers because they came up in the re-examination, additional examination of the witness. And Mr. Nice, in the cross-examination, did raise the question. So they are two documents, two exhibits. One is of a public character, the press conference in February 2000, and the other is the criminal report on the basis of which -- and it is identical with respect to the facts almost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have described them sufficiently to enable the Trial Chamber to find them, and we'll look into the matter. Let the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the documents were returned to me from the ELMO when the cross-examination was stopped. So your officials didn't actually take them. But they were on the ELMO, both these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are in possession of them, of the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were returned to me by the usher from the ELMO when the re-examination was stopped. But before that, General Stevanovic had read both these documents and confirmed their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pass them back through the usher to the clerk and we'll attend to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously if we could have sight of those two, or a copy, if we have any observations to make, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution should have a copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was, incidentally, one document about which I've been minded to ask a supplementary question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My gosh, Mr. Nice. You never lose an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I'll have a -- there's something I wanted to clarify first, and I will, but I may come back on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the exhibits you produced, Mr. Delic, was tab 627. The Chamber doesn't need to go to it. It was a video and its identification is: "Village Osek-Hilj Djakovica (statements by Albanians/Siptars) 13 May 1999." Remind the Chamber of that. Ms. Dicklich will play a short extract.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man whose interview you produced actually identified himself as a doctor. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your exhibit. That's why I asked if you recall.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no doctors there. There were no doctors there. You said Osek-Hilj. He was not a doctor. As far as I could recall, there were two farmers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He said he was a doctor on the video, and he's being located. Can we distribute, for the same purpose as yesterday but this time a written statement. It's not in your own language. Time has not permitted that to happen. Or limited time. But this man you see on this video was seen. He was shown the video. He's given his account of things, and I want your comment on it by reference to some of the things that he's been able to tell us. I shall deal with it quite quickly. First of all, the area with which we are concerned is the same area in general as we were looking at yesterday, which can be seen on page Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 10 of the atlas Exhibit 83. And while -- I'll put mine on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort. No, Mr. Nort. Can we just use this marked copy on the overhead projector. Bottom part. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see on the overhead projector that -- if we could have the overhead projector displayed, please. We can see that he gave an interview, as we already know, in Zim village -- Zjum, rather. Or we will do in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if the Court has its own atlases they'll find it on page 10, because the overhead projector isn't functioning at the moment and I haven't got time to waste -- wait. Ah, there it is. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where we can see at the bottom is the village we were looking at yesterday in the circle. Zjum is just slightly to the north and east of that. So this area would be in the same area as that of the commander you spoke of yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the zone for which my brigade was responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And if we look at the paragraph 24 of this particular statement before we come to the circumstances of the interview, we are informed that on the 31st of March the Serb army, described by this witness as the JNA, but never mind, he no doubt means the VJ, arrived at his village. Is it right that your brigade or part of your brigade arrived at that village on the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This village is in the border area, and my units were constantly in the border area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it right that at that time the purpose of your unit's presence there was to expel the Muslims, in particular Muslims from the Cakaj neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is completely incorrect. These are your insinuations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you please. Do we have any contemporaneous record of what your group was doing -- or, sorry, this battalion was doing on the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, you took my war diary in an illegal manner, so you were able to read what it says there about this battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, I'll not allow you to say that. If that work had been done illegally, the Chamber would have prevented it. You did say, and I recall, that the Prosecutor could look at your diary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said he could look at it but not take it away. He could have asked for it through the Defence and he would have received it without any problem in a completely legal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall several things about this document apart from the fact that it's been the subject of a request for many years that's never been answered. It was produced in court at my request through the Court. It was made available to me for inspection through the Court, and at the end of the day it was handed back to the Court and it wasn't kept by us overnight. I'd quite like to have it back now, please, so I could view it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I notice the recurring approach of the witness. I've told him already I don't mind what he says, but no doubt the Chamber will accept that his observations are effectively challenged when they impute ill-purpose to me, but it's a matter for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, at the moment all I know is that there's no reference or there may be no reference in your war diary to events on the 31st of March. We haven't had time to look at it in detail. Please help me: Is there any contemporaneous record here from the battalion that went to Zjum on or about the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No battalion went to Zjum. Zjum is located in the border area. A border patrol could have entered Zjum, one of the border patrols that patrolled the border daily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we have any contemporaneous document of a border patrol going to Zjum on about the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably does exist in the unit that was responsible for this part of the state border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, the material coming to us suggests that four people were called at Cakaj - or it may be Cakaj, I'm not sure - on about that date. If your troops, border patrol or otherwise, would have been involved in the killing of four people, there should be a contemporaneous record, shouldn't there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Had they taken part in that, there would have been a record of it. But your knowledge stems from statements taken a few days ago. I do not wish to comment at all on those statements. I've already explained the way in which statements are taken on Kosovo -- in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Zjum was a village that contained Kosovo Albanians of the Catholic persuasion, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are in the majority there, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so when the Muslim Kosovo Albanians had been kicked out, or to some extent killed, what was left was Kosovo Albanian Catholics who could be relied on for propaganda purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your statement is absolutely untrue that someone was expelled and that someone was killed because they were a Muslim. As for Catholic Albanians, they did not join the KLA and they respected the state authorities of Serbia. They did not participate in the smuggling of weapons, they did not cross the border to get weapons, and they never attacked army units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of their position, they felt vulnerable in the course of the NATO bombing, didn't they? They felt vulnerable not least because they might be accused by KLA of being cooperators with the Serbs. They were not kicked out, they were favoured, and they were then liable to be thought of as collaborators; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could see it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why when told, as this man told us he was told, that they had to go and take part in protests against the NATO bombing by members of the armed forces, they simply did as they were told. Paragraph 30. Is that right, that they would be used as fodder for demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely untrue. Mr. Nice, for two days you have been giving me documents that are not in my language, and then you refer to paragraphs in those documents. I feel this is improper. I'm not being enabled to give my responses in the proper way. I want to have every document you are using in my own language. I don't wish to work in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General. General, that's a matter for the Chamber to deal with. If you feel you're disadvantaged, what we will do is have the document placed on the ELMO, paragraph 30, and the interpreters will interpret it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort. Can we give a copy to Mr. Nort. Paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 30 of this man's statement reads: "I also remember that sometimes during NATO bombing we were ordered by JNA officer, I do not know the name, to get organised and attend a protest in Prizren against NATO bombing. I also had to join this protest." Now, that's the sort of things, or if I may put it in the vernacular, tricks, it was possible for the armed forces to get up to at that time.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say. I reject it utterly. He speaks of the JNA here. The JNA had not been in existence for years at that point, and army officers had far more important things to do than to organise protest rallies. I think this makes no sense at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Mr. Nort would be good enough to place paragraphs 7 and 8 on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wish to be told on what days these protest rallies that you're mentioning were organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It may be that the person concerned didn't write it in his diary, but I'm not in a position to give you a precise date. Shall we look at paragraph 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is very important to me. I know whether or not there were protests in Prizren and when they took place. We can't talk about something that happened without mentioning a date. I demand to know the date of those protest rallies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, it's not for you, I think, to make demands. You must understand that people have varied recollections of events. But your suggestion that you're entitled to things, is that a way of avoiding answering questions because you don't find them comfortable questions to answer?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questions are not uncomfortable at all. You know I'm willing to answer every question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's press on. The witness -- not the witness, the person says the following: "I recall the time when I gave this interview in Zjum village to the people, who introduced themselves as being from Radio-TV Prizren. I never met any of them before. I do not remember the exact date of the interview, but I think that the date on the title of the video clip, reading May 1999, might be correct." Mr. Delic, I'm not going to demand it, but can you give me the precise date of the interview?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date on the videotape is the right date. There's no reason for there to be any other date there, and it is the editor of the TV programme who stands by that date, and there were other people present there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 8: "The interview had been taken by persons in the JNA -" well, you've made your point about that - "uniforms. They were not armed, but in the nearby cafeteria just 10 metres away from the place where I was interviewed were sitting three policemen, and they were armed. Before the TV crew showed up in the village, I was just sitting in this cafeteria. They approached the above-mentioned policemen and I heard, as they were explaining to the policemen that they are from TV Prizren, that they would like to interview with somebody from our village. They did not mention what they would like to ask our villagers. I never saw any of these persons before. One of them introduced himself as being Sokol Qysja from Prizren." Pausing there, do you know Sokol Qysja?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Sokol Qysja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is the president of an Albanian party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on. He said: "Good afternoon, gentlemen. I am Sokol Qysja from Prizren. How are you doing, are you having any problems? "One the policemen addressed them to me, saying, 'He is a doctor,' and then one of the policemen told: 'Doctor, go and give an interview.' I did not dare to refuse from fear of potential consequences. I was afraid that they could arrest me and later execute me. Following is explanation of my fears." Well, now, this is a doctor. Do you have any reason to doubt you that he was in fear in the circumstances in which he found himself?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would the doctor be afraid of people from the local television station, the president of an Albanian party and policemen, state organs securing the village? There was absolutely no reason for that doctor to be afraid, and you can see that in the interview he gave. He gave the interview quite openly and without any fear at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remember the doctor's interview now. You didn't remember that he was a doctor before, did you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned the name of a different village at first. You didn't mention Zjum. You mentioned Osek Pasa [phoen] and Osek Kia [phoen], and the people there were farmers, not doctors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll press on as quickly as you allow it to be done. If you look at -- if we look at paragraphs 10 and 11, we can read them in full if it's absolutely necessary, but this person makes it clear that Sokol Qysja was advancing the rumour or the suspicion that the doctor had been assisting the KLA. Did you hear any rumours from this man you knew, Sokol Qysja, that a doctor in Zjum had been treating the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apparently Ms. Dicklich says there are two clips in 627, 627 and 627A, and I may have read the description from the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has quite accurately stated the way in which the matter was introduced to him, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we turn on to what he says is the consequence of this for the questions that he was asked in this interview, he says at paragraph 15 that he was interviewed, or he was asked provoking questions but he was not forced or told the answers that he had to give. Do you understand that? He was careful to avoid potential conflict with the Serbian police. Does that seem to you, in the setting of the environment you knew, to be a reasonable attitude for a person in this position to take?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no fear providing the doctor was merely doing his job in his own village. He had no reason to fear contact with our state police. And I ask that the tape be played again so that we can see whether he looks frightened or not and how he is answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you a question earlier, didn't I, about whether Kosovo Albanian Catholics might feel vulnerable, not least because they might be accused of being collaborators, and you said yes they could see it that way. Do you not think there was any vulnerability on the part of witnesses of this kind, or people of this kind, to the pressures of armed police or military?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were completely loyal citizens of the state. There was never any pressure exerted on them. On the contrary, all state organs were especially attentive to those villages and those people and sent them humanitarian aid and every other kind of assistance, because we felt that by remaining on that -- in that territory they would be susceptible to problems because the KLA would consider them to be collaborators, and I understand their fears in this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you made allegations yesterday, which you barely withdrew, about the way in which interviews are conducted and about the objectives of the Office of the Prosecutor. You'll be interested to note the following: On paragraphs 20, 21, and 22, the doctor sets out the questions and answers that he gave and says he has no comments on either the questions or the answers. You see? He accepts that he said those things and doesn't wish to qualify them. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say the witness made allegations yesterday, do you mean yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour when, he was talking about the circumstances in which the woman was interviewed by us. Yes, went to great lengths. I'm reminded of the terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The went to great lengths was the fact that you had organised at short notice a visit to try to locate witnesses. But you took that as some sort of criticism, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That and other passages I did. Indeed, I made an observation at one stage. I'm sorry, I don't have my finger on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you see, if we look at this, the witness accepts some of his answers; third, fourth, and fifth answer. He gives explanations about the first and second questions, and I'll just give you an example of those. He says as to the first question in which he answered -- we're all -- this is paragraph 17: "... in here we're all alive living, police is here as well. We do not have any problems." He says this: "Since the entire Muslims from Prizren HAS province were expelled, we as the Catholic Albanians were ordered to stay in the village against our will. For that reason we didn't feel comfortable, because it compromised us in Muslims population eyes as Serbian collaborators. The order came from a man called Tun Tomrecaj that all Catholics from the village have to stay." Is he right about that, do you know, a man called Tun Tomrecaj ordered them all to stay?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely never have I heard of that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if we move on to the last passage that I want you to help us with, which is the sixth question on paragraph 23, he says this: "The sixth question was 'What about the ones that are bombing?' My answer was: 'What shall I wish for them? All is evil.'" He goes on to say: "My comments to this question and my answering are that the question was obviously provocative. If I was not afraid I would like to say NATO bombing welcome. I heard about many of Serbian armed forces brutalities on the territory of Kosovo before and during NATO bombing, so that is logical I could never support the Serbian policy. In addition, I experienced some evil in our villages, which I would like to put in my statement." And I've dealt with that. So you see, he explains his answer in terms of the pressure that he was under. Did you not appreciate when you produced these videos that they were produced by armed -- not armed, uniformed journalists in circumstances where people would be frightened to give truthful accounts?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, you're asking someone about something happened in 1992, and you're putting the questions in a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1999, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and you're asking them that in 2005. You know what kind of human rights and freedoms there are in Kosovo and how people can speak about certain matters. I ask the Trial Chamber for three things: Yesterday through your witness's statement you levelled serious accusations against my unit and therefore against me personally. I only ask for permission to have telephone contact with the persons who were there on the spot and to ask them in the course of today or tomorrow to send me their statements. Secondly, I ask that the transcript you had here yesterday, together with the video material, be delivered because I cannot pass over it, because I have certain memories connected with that woman which alter completely the story you told here yesterday. And in order to initiate these proceedings before a special court, I need this. So either you can hand it to me or it can be done through the special court in Belgrade, and I only want to make a few telephone calls to the persons who were there on the ground, on the spot. As my recollections have to be confirmed by others, I don't want to put them before the Trial Chamber before having had a chance to verify them, and they refer to that woman. If you remember, the 14th of April is the day when NATO bombed a column between Djakovica and Prizren. This television crew that was filming this event, after the event went and filmed the bombing of this column. I recall some things that I learned that evening, but I wish to call the direct participants in that event before telling the Court what my recollections are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, my observation on that is if there are exist -- I don't know what he means by statements. If there are existing documents that he asserts would assist the Chamber, then the associates of the accused, acting in the role of solicitors or lawyers or advocates, could contact the people concerned for production of the documents, but that for the Chamber to accept in any form hearsay statements via the telephone from other participants would be unusual if not completely irregular.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is not asking to submit statements. He explained very clearly that what he wants is to reinforce his own memory and to double-check it. I think that his request for having the possibility of making telephone calls granted to him are very well-founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, it would be very unusual to allow a witness during his testimony to make telephone calls in relation to that testimony. On the other hand, the accused has heard what you have said and the associates have also heard, and it is a matter for them to take the matter further if they can. Proceed, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Robinson. Since I cannot contact persons who help the accused, I would have to tell someone who should be called. Do I have permission to speak to the legal advisors so that they call these persons? I know what I will do when I return to Belgrade in connection with this case, because then it will remain as Mr. Nice presented it and as it stands now, but I don't believe that's the way it was. So could I please have permission to contact one of the associates from the Defence so that they carry this through?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Delic, very exceptionally the Chamber will allow you to contact one of the associates for that very limited purpose and that purpose alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we turn from this topic, your answer, or your observation as translated was you asked if you could have the transcript because you have certain memories connected with that woman which alter completely the story you told here yesterday. Please answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't know if that's a fair representation. The story that was represented, that was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm reading out exactly the transcript. He meant -- by "you" he meant she.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confine your question to yes or no, please. Are you saying that you now have active memories of that particular woman? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke very precisely yesterday, and that's what I meant. I never saw that woman in my life and that's why I cannot remember her. However, something in connection with her, something that I need to have confirmed, that's what I have on my mind and that is why I need to contact people who were on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You better tell me -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All night I've --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You better tell me what it is, but before you do, since you now have some memory, remember that part of the evidence was given in private session and part in public. Is this appropriate for public or private session?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's nothing particularly secret about this in order to require private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what this memory is that's come to you connected to, as you described, that woman.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that until I check it, because I do not want to deal with half-truths here. This thing that crossed my mind, I want to check it out. I want to check whether it's that woman, and it's only people who were on the spot that can tell me. It has to do with the request that that woman on that day presented a -- presented on that day to the people there during the filming. So I'm just wondering whether it was that woman or another woman and whether we acted on that request of hers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now what is the request that you now recollect a woman making?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's just what I've been saying. I want to check it. I want to check my memory to see whether it's correct. I do not want to present a request now that I cannot confirm, that I can confirm only later, having spoken to these persons. Maybe it had to do with another woman. I do not want to deceive the Trial Chamber here in any way. The legal associates are going to call whoever necessary, and the Trial Chamber will probably allow for me to hear from them what they were told, and then I will know more about this request and my memory in relation to this woman. I cannot present half-truths here. It's been many years now, and I have to check my own memory, whether it is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't there yourself so you're going to be seeking to produce something that somebody else says, yes?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My officers who were there themselves, the cameraman who was there, and the editor who was there, and something that one of my officers said to me during the course of those few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, your credibility is in issue here, and I will be grateful, please, now for an answer to the question. What memory of a request by a woman do you have that you think may be material? I'd like to hear it before you have access to documentation and make your own decision about whether you're going to add to your evidence. So can I know, please, what it is that you say you've recollected?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are now asking me to say something that I'm not certain of. That is very unfair. I have just asked the Trial Chamber to make these telephone calls in order to confirm whether what I remember pertains to this woman or another woman. So I don't want to say one thing today and to say tomorrow that what I said on this day was not correct, and you persist and you keep invoking my credibility. I realise that you have a problem and I realise that you're trying to challenge my credibility therefore, but that's a completely different matter. You are within your rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's up to the Chamber whether the Chamber requires him to answer the question. In the circumstances, it's, in my submission, an entirely reasonable request and one that he should comply with. It's not up to a witness, as it were, to choose to add or not to his evidence in these circumstances, but I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you're talking about a recollection of something being said by a woman, and in your mind there's the possibility of two women; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been thinking whether it's this woman from this village or another woman from another village. It is for that reason that the legal advisors should call the people who were on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the other village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other village, I think it's the area of the village of Lipovac. That is further to the west ten or 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but it's probably been written down, the name of the woman who spoke on television, because as you can see, on TV there were always captions stating the name. And as far as this other woman is concerned, her name must be recorded too. But right now I cannot say with any degree of certainty which one of the two women is involved. Perhaps it's the other one, but perhaps it's this one. At any rate, what is characteristic is that both women were from Bosnia, and their request had to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in the circumstances we consider it reasonable for the witness to adopt the position that he has.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 629, please. We'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness make his inquiries to the associates at the earliest possible moment, because it's not a topic I want to let go of, and I want to know what the final position is from him. May he make those inquiries perhaps at the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you may make your inquiries through the associates at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if that is the way to deal with this, Mr. Nice. I'm thinking aloud, but what I had envisaged when it was raised was that the information would be obtained by Mr. Milosevic's associates for re-examination purposes and the matter would be dealt with that way rather than the witness be briefed for the purpose of his evidence. I wasn't envisaging that there would be a two-way communication of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I completely object to being excluded from the possibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I'm conscious of what would then concern you and it seems to me a matter on which you would be entitled to come back, if it was necessary, to explore it fully. But if you're saying that there should be a two-way communication with the associates, then that may be appropriate, but it certainly would be very, very unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if this witness wishes, in the way the Chamber has now allowed, to amplify his recollection and if it comes out that his amplified recollection relates to this woman, I want to hear about it obviously at the earliest possible moment so I can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll proceed as indicated. Yes, as I indicated, the witness can speak to the associates at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 629, again we needn't look at it, but the surrogate sheet in the binder describes it as the video segment concerning "Albanians, Turks and Roma in VJ units, April 1999." Can we look at a short extract of that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause there for a minute. Your Honours, apart from the doctor who was identified, none of the people, I think, apart from the party leader referred to by the witness, Sokol Qysja, is identified. We have identified a total of three people, the doctor and two others, and we are making all the results of our inquiries available. On the screen now is one of the men in this trench-digging video, and I distribute for cross-examination purposes a statement. It does identify him by name and he has no objection to his name being known. Mihill Bezhi. Again we'll lay it on the overhead projector as far as necessary, very swiftly, it won't take long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Catholic Albanian explains in paragraph 2 that he became a member of the SPS between 1995 and 1999 just in order not to lose his job and because of the promise that he would get a flat. Is that the sort of thing that was happening in this state in that period of time, that membership of the political party of this accused was either necessary for retention of jobs and/or beneficial in bringing things like flats?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect. My family had several members who worked in Kosovo, too, and not a single member of my family ever got a flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 explains that he was shown the video clip and that he says in paragraph 4 he remembers the time in April 1999 when he gave the interview. Help me, Mr. Delic, with the precise date of the interview.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should be on the video clip itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... April 1999. Can you give me the precise date?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the precise date, but, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. He says: "I remember the time in April 1999 when I gave interview on this video to a Serbian journalist Ugrinovic." That's the man, isn't it? Ugrinovic is your --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I do not recall his first name. Ugrinovic was wearing JNA military uniform." Yes. Well, we know about JNA. He was -- but first of all, it's right, isn't it? Journalists wore uniform. It may not be that surprising, but it's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all journalists wore uniform. Ugrinovic, among other things, was on the list of reservists of the army of Yugoslavia, but at the request of the local self-government he was freed from this duty in order to be able to do his own work. If necessary, he could have been called back to his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just staying with that and diverting, digressing for one minute. Is it also right, as we've heard in paragraph 94 of an expert's report -- it's not before you, a Mr. de la Brosse, a Frenchman. Is it also right, as we've heard, that soldiers were posted in the offices of media companies in order to keep reporting under control? Is that right, as he has told us?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. No soldiers of the army of Yugoslavia or of my unit had anything to do with the media. It was only people who were employed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll press on, then, with paragraph 5: "I didn't give the above mentioned statement voluntarily, but under pressure of current circumstances, which means, that if I didn't give the interview, I was told, that I would be fired from my job. The person who forced me to give the interview was Sokol Qysja from Prizren." And he is shown indeed on this video. "Sokol is the only person who gave interview on the video clip voluntarily as a president of the Albanian Reform Party with pro-Serbian policy orientation." Now, first of all it's right, isn't it, that Sokol Qysja has a pro-Serbian orientation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sokol Qysja belonged to those Albanians who respected the state authorities of the Republic of Serbia and who did their own jobs. He had a party of his own, I don't know its name. As far as Prizren is concerned, he had quite a few members. So it is not true that he was of a pro-Serb orientation. He presented the views of the Albanians, and there is nothing that would lead to the conclusion that he was pro-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was oriented towards a co-existence, a joint life between Serbs and Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 explains that that man Sokol Qysja visited the director of Liria shop, a man called Alexandar Kamparevic who called Mihill Bezhi to the office, saying give a statement or you will be fired or we will take you to dig trenches. So this man who has three children had little option but to agree to give the statement. Do you accept that as a possibility? It was the territory upon which you were work. Tell us, might this have happened?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This absolutely could not have happened the way you are putting it. This man was already in the army units. There is no Sokol Qysja that could have taken this soldier to see his director. He would have to get permission from the military organs to leave the unit. The man you're mentioning here Alexandar Kamparevic was the director of Liria. I don't know what kind of relationship he had with Sokol Qysja. But for someone to be able to take soldiers from the front line in order to have pressure exerted upon them by somebody else is something that I challenge in its totality, because from the moment they joined the ranks of the army of Yugoslavia, it was only the army of Yugoslavia that was responsible for them. And after all, what he says here is stated in his statement too. In the units you could not have civilians strolling about. As far as I know, this director Kamparevic never came to the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, he goes on to explain that on the same day he went to Vrbnica village with Sokol Qysja and two journalists and a cameraman. It's about 17 kilometres from Prizren. When he got there, there were about a hundred to 200 people in uniform in a yard and in a house. While he was in the house he heard somebody being interviewed giving answers as directed by Sokol Qysja, and he then goes on to explain that an officer told him, Mihill Bezhi, to put on a military jacket and he gave the statement which was written for him on the spot, being held by Sokol Qysja so that he could read it. That's his account, you see. Very detailed. Any reason -- might it be correct, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, this soldier, this reservist, is wearing an old type of uniform. M77 is that uniform. Soldiers were already wearing M89 uniforms. So there was no one to give him that uniform that you are referring to because all soldiers were already wearing these more modern uniforms, M89 and M93, whereas he is wearing the old type of uniform, as I see here, M77. As for this man that you interviewed, I do not support what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one more short one to go, Your Honours, but I observe the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have one more?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have another statement to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On tab 627, this man was seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you just play a small section of it, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you remember this man, Mr. Delic, and the interview of him that you produced?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do remember that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Distribute, please, a statement he's made. Now, this man from Zjum eventually in his statement gives some of the history. I'm going to deal with it very shortly. Paragraph 12. He says this, that shortly after the NATO bombing, the first Serbian military formations appeared in his village, and he would describe them as of paramilitary appearance. He remembers that they arrived at the Cakaj neighbourhood, which is sort of part of or detached from his village where they forced the population out and then burnt three or four houses. Sorry, burnt nearly all of the houses apart from three or four that were left. Do you have any recollection of houses in Cakaj being burnt?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was a paramilitary group or something that looked like a paramilitary group in your area of responsibility at that time, what would they be? Help us, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area there would be no paramilitary groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If so, it would have to be a military group, and therefore it would be under your command; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would mean that all the groups that were within that border belt were groups which were under the command of the army. And they weren't groups, they were units, whether larger or smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course the commission, the VJ commission of which you were -- or with which you worked in preparation for this trial didn't prepare documents in relation to what happened at the area of Zjum at about this time, did it? You don't have any documents at all that cover it.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because in that area nothing unusual was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's see what he says. We press on rapidly. He says that on paragraph 15, his recollection is that Serbian regular army appeared the same day as paramilitary and burnt houses in the Cakaj neighbourhood, and he recognised six Serbian JNA military jeeps but couldn't see how many soldiers there were although they were passing his house. Right? But a deployment of a unit with six jeeps is something that should be recorded, shouldn't it, in the records of your part of the army, your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my brigade I was the only one who had a jeep, and my military police another jeep. So that's makes a total of two jeeps at the level of the whole brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could this be the police working together with the army on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did not come closer to the border belt except the villages that were on the fringes of the border belt, and this particular village was within the border belt. And the police didn't launch any operations in those villages at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says the soldiers told us not to leave the village and not to allow any Muslims into their houses and made it clear that if they didn't obey that order, they would have their houses burned and they would be killed. Can you think of any of your unit commanders who might have broken rank or broken your rules to do that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your observation that they broke my orders. My commanders, on the other hand, had very precise orders, and I have no knowledge or I'm not aware that anybody took it upon themselves to violate the order. So this is a statement that was taken in 2005, and let me repeat once again, in Kosovo in 2005 was when the statement was taken, and you cannot get a different type of statement in Kosovo except for the one corresponding to the present balance of forces in Kosovo and the present situation in Kosovo. Now, I have no intention of being angry at this man who gave the statement, or any other person who gave you any statements at all, because I know full well that if they wish to live in Kosovo they must need give statements of this kind which correspond to the present state of affairs and the present situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the detail he's already given, in paragraph 17 he deals with the four deaths that the earlier statement spoke of, and he gives the names: Ibrahim Mallakaj, Agron Cekaj, Mesar Cakaj, and Ali Tanushaj. He actually identifies four people killed by armed forces at that time. You're unable to give us any account of how those people died, are you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. If there is knowledge of that kind, then the witness should have told you whether they were members of the KLA, for instance, whether they were carrying weapons, whether they were trying to cross the state border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He then goes on, and this is the last background matter that I need deal with and I'll try to deal with it quickly, at paragraph 20 and subsequently, to what he described as paramilitary soldiers entered his house, abused him in foul language, and then at paragraph 21, he being there with his wife and daughters, he was forced out, made to lie on the ground, had a boot, I think, put on his body and certainly the butt of a rifle or Kalashnikov on his back and then the barrel onto his back. His family were made to come out, although paragraph 25 suggests not and until his daughter Bernadetta had been told to hand over her necklace, otherwise they would take it together with her head. So this is a case of gross, terrifying violence used against a family. Do you allow that as a possibility by your troops, please?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I don't allow any kind of possibility like that. Would the interpreter interpret paragraph 23 for me, please, translate the paragraph, especially the last portion of paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're coming to that in a minute. I'm dealing with things in sequence, and if you will be good enough to let me deal with the questioning, we'll get on much quicker that way. You see, he then says that as his family had come out, he was lying on the ground for about five or ten minutes and they ordered him to stand up, make him go to the main gate of the yard where he met his wife and two daughters. They then went to the house of the neighbour Zef Lekaj and there were gathered people from the neighbourhood in one room, about 22 people, and he was told by this armed group, "You are lucky that we belong to --" now the way it's appeared in the text at the moment with a rush -- not a rush translation but a translation by a non-English speaker, but it's been translated to: "You are lucky that we belong to the Medetirian group and we are not members of the Arkan group, otherwise we would kill you..." What does "Medetirian group" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that this is an absolute lie. In my zone no paramilitary group was allowed in because they would have to settle accounts with my military police and my army first of all. And I've been repeating that for hundreds of times. Hundreds of times I've heard mention about this Arkan group and for the first time this Mediterranean group, or whatever it is. There was none of that in my zone. It was strictly forbidden by an order of the corps command, and here during the trial we read out that order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the Medetirian group work?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group was just working and functioning in the mind of this witness. The group didn't exist on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you've never heard of it before or anything similar to it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've heard about hundreds of groups but this is the first time that I hear of a group with this name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He then deals with other matters that we've covered already, but it's with that background that he deals with the circumstances of his making his statement. And we can find that on paragraph 6 and 7. He explains that in paragraph 6 he doesn't remember the date but he thinks it's after the beginning of the NATO airstrike. He says that he was driving his car from Karashengjergj to Zjum village on that day. Upon arrival to the village he was stopped by men in Serbian military camouflage uniform, and in paragraph 8, his detailed account is this: That he was addressed in the Albanian language, told he had to give an interview in the Albanian language about his opinion of NATO bombing, replied that his Albanian language wasn't good and he would prefer to give the interview in the Serbo-Croat language. No reason to doubt any of that, is there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he says. I can't know one way or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us quite a lot about how good the journalists are, and you knew them quite well by name. See if you can help us with the next bit. He reads on the microphone that the journalist had in his hand Pristina TV. The man claimed he was a journalist from TV Pristina although he'd never seen him before. The journalist was in the company of two police officers and another two journalists in Serbian military uniforms. So there's one in civilians and two in uniform. Apart from the policeman, nobody else was armed. He didn't recognise any of the people, and they spoke Albanian. Any reason to doubt any of that detail?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do have reason, because as far as these journalists are concerned, the ones I know, they don't speak Albanian. Second, you mentioned Television Pristina twice here, so those journalists couldn't have said that because those journalists belong to Television Serbia but the studio in Prizren, if that refers to the same case at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Then he says he gave -- and he says no more than this, Mr. Delic, this man. He says: "I gave the interview as I assumed they would like to hear it, at the benefit of the pro-Serbian policy in Kosovo. I did it from fear that something wrong might happen to me or my family. Since I have already explained on my own Serbian police and military behaviour in our village." No doubt he discussed that before the statement itself was prepared. "But during the interview they did not use any kind of pressure on me," he says, "to give such comments about NATO bombing in Kosovo." He doesn't suggest they exerted pressure. He suggests that it was his own fear in all the circumstances that made him say what he did. Now, you told me at the beginning how these people would have some anxieties. Do you not allow the possibility of somebody saying that and doing that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as he had fears then to give an interview, he has today when he gave an interview for you, those same anxieties or, rather, your investigators. The anxiety and fear is the same, perhaps even greater now. So now too he has to think about all this and to hit the target to see whether what he's going to say corresponds to what those people asking for the interview want to hear. So as you interpreted this for me, he therefore observed that he gave an interview pursuant his own free will, he wasn't forced to do so, but that he himself assessed what kind of interview he was supposed to give and which interview would correspond to the prevailing situation. When he gave you the interview, he also wanted to see that the interview was not detrimental to himself and his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... topic of free will can be found at paragraph 28, where he says this: "I would like to say that the interview I gave to the journalist as recorded on video clip tab 627, had nothing to do with my own will, likewise in other above mentioned cases where we were directly or indirectly forced to do it." You see, Mr. Delic, I'm going to suggest to you that the investigators of the ICTY, or the investigator, in response to the material you've produced, displays the following, and I ask your final comments on it: That the oppression and history of violence of the forces in Kosovo by the time of the NATO bombing was such that people knew they had to say what was wanted of them. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not acceptable and not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was always possible for journalists, especially in uniform and with the presence of police and military, to have a good chance of getting what they wanted without using force?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The journalists are professionals, and as such they do their job professionally, and they wouldn't have jeopardised their professional ethics because there was no need to do so. Mr. Nice, the truth is only one. There is only one truth. Therefore you can't reach the truth through force. And as for the freedom of the press today in Kosovo, there is a lot of information and facts that you can arrive at, check them out and see what kind of freedom of movement exists in Kosovo today and what kind of freedom of the press and freedom of expression exists today there. See for yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... seen with these four people who we've reviewed yesterday and today in reverse order is an escalator of pressure, from the pressure of historical circumstances and the circumstances themselves through the suggestion that you'll lose your job if you don't comply, through more direct pressure right up to the terrible pressure applied to that woman, as you describe her. And you must know in your position and in the state in which you were living that those things were going on.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying now is just not correct. People at that time, even if it was true that they could lose their jobs, for example, today can lose their heads if they don't give the kind of statements they're expected to give. So it's not the same. To lose your job or to lose your head are two quite different things because today people lose their heads much more frequently in Kosovo today than during the time when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two other points. Have you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. While we're on this statement, I think it would be necessary for Mr. Nice to tell us what the name of the group that was mentioned here in fact is, because what it says here, Medetirian, doesn't mean anything. It doesn't mean anything in Serbian and it means nothing in English either, or any other language. So nobody can understand why somebody would call a group by a name that means nothing. And his investigators were the people who collected that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that is the term which is in the text. I don't know whether that can be improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Classic example of the investigators acting with neutrality and recording what they're told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the topic of groups, and you'd heard so many hundred names in Kosovo, what did you hear of the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about -- I mostly heard about the Skorpions lately, that it was a group that was active in Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And following this trial --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I knew nothing about them in Kosovo, during the war period. And let me repeat once again, paramilitary groups could not enter my zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what about other zones? Why were they able to enter other zones?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they could enter other zones. The orders by the corps commander related to all brigade commanders. But what I'm talking about is my own zone because I was responsible only for my own area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard of the Skorpions being reactivated for Kosovo. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I followed the trial when the Skorpions were mentioned, so I know what was said in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally, I take it, you haven't made your phone call so far to deal with the bit of evidence about the woman, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no, he may not have been able to. It's only the one break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he wasn't to make the phone call --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're quite right. Very well. I just want to know as soon as we get the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now turn back, then, to a few of the crime sites very rapidly -- or not very rapidly but fairly swiftly. And if we can go to tab 361. Volume, I think, 5. Yes, volume 5 in the English version. We have to start, actually, at 360 just to remind ourselves that the material that you provide is this. This freshly drawn map, I mean freshly drawn or recently drawn map. As a matter of fact, when were these maps -- I'm so sorry. Materials you provide are this map, 360. When were these maps actually drawn?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that they are not maps dating back to the time when the events took place. They are maps dating to 2002. And their purpose is to help explain the events, as required by the Commission for Cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then we see things like 361, your statement, and then we see the statement of Vukovic who we know was in the area of the -- who was in charge of the battalion that was dealing with the area we were just recently looking at, and various other statements. Now, so far as Bela Crkva is concerned, a great deal of evidence has been given about it from various people; Fehim Elshani, Isuf Jemini, Sabri Popaj, to name three. Do you know anything adverse to those people as individuals?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anything linked to those people at all, and I don't know them, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the commission, the VJ commission, whether it investigated these people or not, turned up nothing about them or adverse to them despite having all the opportunities since 2002 to look into them if it wanted to; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a total lack of understanding of the situation under which the commission works. The commission had absolutely no chance of contacting those individuals at all. The commission could not go to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and the commission first and foremost dealt with members of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... exhaustive records, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All they could have had were records in possession of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've heard evidence of Serb police soldiers, as I think they's described, but also Serb police and army entering the village on the 25th of March, and of some 400 or thereabouts villagers gathering in the stream, walking towards Rogova. Do you say that evidence is possibly true, partly true, or definitely untrue?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time? What was the time when this happened?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can't necessarily expect time, but it so happens that one of the witnesses said about 4.00 in the morning the police and army started shooting towards the village, looting and burning the houses, and it was in those circumstances that the villagers fled in diverse directions until about 400 of them gathered and went along the stream. So if 4.00 in the morning helps you, tell us, please. And this is the 25th of March, I think before your war diary starts, probably.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's very important to me when you tell me the exact time and date. I can now say that this is absolutely untrue, because the soldiers entered that village in a column at around 500 hours, as can be seen from the statements, and you can see from the map that no blockade or search of the village of Bela Crkva had been envisioned. The troops marched through the village in a column, and it was only when they reached the hill of Amovac, the next feature, that they spread out and set up the blockade line. Bela Crkva was not considered because there was a police checkpoint there, because the main road between the village of Zrze and Orahovac passed through it, and because there was security there to prevent attacks on vehicles passing through. It was estimated that there were no KLA members in Bela Crkva and that therefore there was no need to enter the village. So they only marched through the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The difference between 5.00 and 4.00 is not so great when the witness concerned says "about 4.00." The description of shooting and burning of houses, are you saying that this is necessarily a complete invention because your troops would have seen it and recorded it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm testifying here about the period from the 25th to the 28th inclusive. As I said previously, I passed through this village several -- on several more occasions up to the 4th of April. This could not have happened in the village of Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we've heard from a witness by the name, or by the pseudonym of K25. He's a member of the PJP. Have you considered his evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement was not shown to me, and I have not had an opportunity to read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. He explains how it was at about five to six that with the PJP from the 23rd Detachment, deployed from Zrze to Mala Krusa, Velika Krusa, and then from Zrze to Bela Crkva. Now, was there any involvement of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the PJP participated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do, then, on the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained this here, and it's in the maps. They had their position in the blockade line, and they had their tasks in fighting the terrorist 124th Brigade or parts of it. It was no longer just a group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how do you say people died in Bela Crkva that day, if you accept that they did at all?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, after all the units had passed through Bela Crkva and set up the blockade line outside Bela Crkva, it was outside the zone of operations. I am not aware that anything occurred there. On the following days, I passed through that part of Bela Crkva through which an asphalt road runs in the direction of Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, and to take it shortly, as you possibly know, there's an account of 14 people being killed by the stream, and that's dealt with in detail as to how that came about; men being separated, men being made to undress and so on. There's other accounts of those bodies being seen, and there's accounts of the bodies being buried, and there's accounts of nearly all the houses being burnt. Is all of this, this evidence, entirely fabricated?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say you have statements. Then we should go through each of them in turn. Mr. Milosevic asked me about this too. I am familiar with this entire territory. I know the village, the stream, the field around the village of Bela Crkva, and as I have already said, would it be logical, instead of going along the stream, into the thickets where one could be concealed from view, or if Bela Crkva is here, to go out into the open field. If people are frightened, they wouldn't go there because they could be easily seen. Instead of going in the direction of Orahovac where there are streams, gullies, various kinds of bushes, hedges, copses of trees where they could hide, although of course there was no reason for them to hide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the stream is quite sunken below the level of the surrounding fields, is it not, providing some form of cover, and consistent with the description that the men were told they had to get down into the river or streambed to undress before they were executed. So in fact, quite a useful way to escape detection.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you ever been there, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not allowed to ask me questions, but you may have noticed that I asked you those details without reference to any documents. I'm right, aren't I? The bridge is rather a flat bridge and there's a sunken stream and it's a stream down into which you can walk, which explains -- let me repeat it for you in case you overlooked, in your focus on finding something to ask me, that they were obliged to get down into the stream and to undress. Now, then, not such a silly way to go by way of an escape route, was it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would go against any kind of logic if one was fleeing. I have been there. I know what this stream looks like. It's also used for irrigation. There is a railway line running across it in one part, but it's in a flat area, a plain where there are fields on which vegetables are grown, and there is nowhere to hide there. In the opposite direction, towards the north, one would find much more favourable conditions for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two other points and then we'll leave Bela Crkva. Just to deal with your last point -- or three other points. Of course, a stream of the kind we've described lying, I think, behind first either some houses and some growth or thickets of some kind might not be something along which a tank could actually run, might it? You can't run along a stream like this in a tank, can you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tanks usually are not driven through streams, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you would be good enough to consider a passage -- I've just relayed to you in very summary form evidence from the live witnesses here who were driven out of their village, they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we now look at "As Seen, As Told," the book prepared by OSCE, in the English version at page 278, and lay that on the overhead projector, please. Perhaps we would just go back to page 277, Mr. Nort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, OSCE conducted its own independent investigation into Bela Crkva in -- into Bela Crkva. And if you look at the page -- I know it's in English but if you look at it, you'll see it starts at footnote 26, and we go to the end of the passage on Bela Crkva it goes to footnote 44.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything here. I don't understand anything it says here. I ask again to be allowed to follow in my own language. You're pulling things out of context here to suit your own purposes. This means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have your copy, the one you believed to have been written by Natasa Kandic, of "As Seen, As Told" with you for these pages?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your allusions have nothing to do with me. I have no copies here, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, if we look just first of all at the passage. It's in English, but whether or not you read English I don't know, but you can follow the format. If we look at the passage that's on the screen, the first footnote is 26. The last footnote is 44. If Mr. Nort now turns on, very briefly, to page 282, we'll see that footnotes 26 to 44 sets out a large number of different -- where it's got A/0234 or A/0490, these are all unique figures identifying people to whom the preparers of this book spoke. And so without counting them up, we can see several, or it may be many, some of who were given detailed footnote references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's barely legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. If we could just focus a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, so between footnote 26 and then footnote 44. You see the way this book was prepared, on the basis of individual -- it may have included some of those relied on by the ICTY, they may have been entirely different. If Mr. Nort comes back, then, to page 277. The research of those preparing this book, and I'll just take you to one passage of detail at the moment, is to this effect. It's on the right-hand side of the page, if we can enlarge it a little. Thank you. It deals with the incident down at the ditch, as it's described in the previous paragraph. "Fifty-five men were separated from the women and children. The women and children were ordered to leave. The 55 men were forced to strip to the waist and stand with their hands behind their head while they were searched. A bullet was found in the pocket of a 13-year-old boy.
